summary:
Orbit Atlas is an interactive map of Mars and the Moon that brings back the robots and spacecraft that were abandoned there. Each forgotten mission appears as a point on the map, and when the user visits it, the project shows information about that robot or spacecraft: what it was, what it was designed to do, and what happened to it. We developed the core in C++ using a weighted graph to connect the mission sites, with Dijkstra’s algorithm and BFS to explore routes between them, and a hash table for fast access to each mission’s data.

This addresses the challenge “Abandoned but not Forgotten” by making sure these discarded missions are remembered and easy to find. It is important because every one of these machines is part of the history of space exploration. By presenting that legacy through an interactive map, Orbit Atlas helps plant the seed of interest in new generations, especially students aged 12 to 15, and increases the number of young people connected to space science and exploration.
details: Orbit Atlas is an interactive map of Mars and the Moon where each abandoned robot or spacecraft appears as a point that, when visited, shows information about that mission: what it was, what it was designed to do, and what happened to it. The map is modeled as a weighted graph, a non-linear data structure in which every mission site is a node and every route between two sites is an edge whose weight represents the distance between them. We implemented the graph ourselves in C++, and it lets us apply Dijkstra’s algorithm to find the shortest path between any two missions, and BFS to discover which sites can be reached from a given point and in how many steps. Alongside the graph, we use a hash table that stores each mission’s information (name, description, status) under a key, so that when a user clicks a point the data is retrieved almost instantly instead of searching through a whole list. Together, the graph handles how missions relate to each other, while the hash table handles what each mission is, and we analyzed the efficiency of both with Big O notation. All of this is connected to a simple HTML interface designed for students aged 12 to 15, with the goal of planting the seed of interest in new generations so that more young people become involved in space science. The project is creative because it turns forgotten machines into places you can discover rather than static data, and we kept a focused minimum viable product and planned tests with edge cases to make sure it works correctly.
